conclusion: Memory effects in multiscale stochastic dynamics can be mitigated by tailored protocols, offering a strategy for controlling relaxation in complex systems.

title: Subgap Pumping Of Antiferromagnetic Mott Insulators: Photoexcitation Mechanisms And Applications
authors: Radu Andrei, Mingyao Guo, Mustafa G Ali, Hoon Kim, Richard D Averitt, David Hsieh And Eugene Demler
abstract: We study the behavior of the 2D repulsive Hubbard model on a square lattice at half filling, under strong driving with ac electric fields, by employing a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach. Within the same theoretical framework, we analytically obtain the conventional Keldysh crossover between multiphoton and tunneling photoexcitation mechanisms, as well as two new regimes beyond the Keldysh paradigm. We discuss how dynamical renormalization of the Mott–Hubbard gap feeds back into the photoexcitation process, modulating the carrier generation rate in real time. The momentum distribution of quasiparticle excitations immediately after the drive is calculated, and shown to contain valuable information about the generation mechanism. Finally, we discuss experimental probing of the pump-induced nonequilibrium electronic state.
tldr: This paper studies photoexcitation mechanisms in antiferromagnetic Mott insulators under strong ac driving, revealing regimes beyond the Keldysh crossover and dynamical gap renormalization.
motivation: Understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated systems is important for both fundamental physics and potential applications in ultrafast control of materials.
method: The authors use a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach to simulate the 2D repulsive Hubbard model at half filling under strong ac electric fields.
result: They analytically derive the conventional Keldysh crossover and identify two new photoexcitation regimes, showing that dynamical renormalization of the Mott gap modulates carrier generation in real time.
conclusion: The momentum distribution of quasiparticles after the drive encodes information about the generation mechanism, and the non-equilibrium state can be probed experimentally.

title: Quantum Entanglement, Stratified Spaces, And Topological Matter: Towards Entanglement-sensitive Langlands Data
authors: Kazuki Ikeda And Steven Rayan
abstract: Using the spinless Haldane model, we study the witness-filtered Berry curvature, quantum geometric tensor, and quantum Fisher information on the gapped strata of the parameter space and evaluate them through the Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki discretization. The filtered quantities isolate the part of the geometric response carried by sublattice coherence: they suppress contributions from regions where the occupied Bloch state is locally A/B-separable and emphasize regions where curvature and coherence coexist. We derive exact lattice identities, reconstruction formulas for the curvature-weighted coherence, and bounds relating the filtered quantum geometric tensor and quantum Fisher information to single-particle mode entanglement. Across the gap-closing stratum, the quantized response changes admit a natural description in terms of Hecke modifications. We elicit a corresponding Langlands viewpoint—not as a full correspondence, but as an organizational principle and as the mathematical shadow of these physical geometric constructions.
tldr: The paper uses geometric and information-theoretic quantities to study entanglement in topological matter, connecting to Langlands theory.
motivation: To understand how quantum entanglement manifests in topological phases and to develop a mathematical framework linking geometry, topology, and information.
method: Applies witness-filtered Berry curvature, quantum geometric tensor, and quantum Fisher information to the Haldane model, using Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki discretization.
result: Derives exact lattice identities and bounds relating filtered geometric quantities to single-particle mode entanglement, and interprets quantized responses via Hecke modifications.
conclusion: The work suggests a Langlands-inspired organizational principle for entanglement in topological matter, but remains a mathematical exploration rather than a direct contribution to quantum information theory.

title: Quantum Cellular Automata On Symmetric Subalgebras
authors: Ruochen Ma, Yabo Li, And Meng Cheng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2123 (2026).

We investigate quantum cellular automata (QCA) on one-dimensional spin systems defined over a subalgebra of the full local operator algebra – the symmetric subalgebra under a finite Abelian group symmetry [MATH]. For systems where each site carries a regular representation of [MATH], we establish a complete classification of such subalgebra QCAs based on two topological invariants: (1) a surjective homomorphism from the group of subalgebra QCAs to the group of anyon permutation symmetries in a [MATH] [MATH] gauge theory; and (2) a generalization of the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner (GNVW) index that characterizes the flow of the symmetric subalgebra. Specifically, two subalgebra QCAs correspond to the same anyon permutation and share the same index if and only if they differ by a finite-depth unitary circuit composed of [MATH]-symmetric local gates. We also identify a set of operations that generate all subalgebra QCAs through finite compositions. As an example, we examine the Kramers-Wannier duality on a [MATH] symmetric subalgebra, demonstrating that it maps to the [MATH]-[MATH] permutation in the two-dimensional toric code and has an irrational index of [MATH]. Therefore, it cannot be extended to a QCA over the full local operator algebra and mixes nontrivially with lattice translations.

.
tldr: Classifies quantum cellular automata on symmetric subalgebras using topological invariants and shows the Kramers-Wannier duality has an irrational index.
motivation: To understand the structure and classification of quantum cellular automata that preserve a symmetry subalgebra, which is a topic in quantum computation theory.
method: Uses algebraic classification with two invariants: anyon permutation symmetry and a generalized GNVW index, and constructs generating operations.
result: Establishes a complete classification of subalgebra QCAs and demonstrates that the Kramers-Wannier duality cannot be extended to a full QCA.
conclusion: Subalgebra QCAs are classified by anyon permutations and an index, with nontrivial examples like the Kramers-Wannier duality.

title: Squeezing Enhancement In Lossy Multi-Path Atom Interferometers
authors: Julian Günther, Jan-Niclas Kirsten-Siemß, Naceur Gaaloul, And Klemens Hammerer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2122 (2026).

This paper explores the sensitivity gains afforded by spin-squeezed states in atom interferometry, in particular using Bragg diffraction. We introduce a generalised input-output formalism that accurately describes realistic, non-unitary interferometers, including losses due to velocity selectivity and scattering into undesired momentum states. This formalism is applied to evaluate the performance of one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states in improving phase sensitivity. Our results show that by carefully optimising the parameters of the Bragg beam splitters and controlling the degree of squeezing, it is possible to improve the sensitivity of the interferometer by several dB with respect to the standard quantum limit despite realistic levels of losses in light pulse operations. However, the analysis also highlights the challenges associated with achieving these improvements in practice, most notably the impact of finite temperature on the benefits of entanglement. The results suggest ways of optimising interferometric setups to exploit quantum entanglement under realistic conditions, thereby contributing to advances in precision metrology with atom interferometers.

.
tldr: This paper studies sensitivity enhancement using spin-squeezed states in lossy atom interferometers, focusing on practical metrology rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Atom interferometers are limited by the standard quantum limit; spin squeezing can improve sensitivity but is degraded by losses and finite temperature.
method: The authors develop a generalized input-output formalism for non-unitary interferometers including velocity selectivity and scattering losses, and apply it to one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states.
result: Optimizing Bragg beam splitter parameters and squeezing degree yields several dB improvement over the standard quantum limit despite realistic losses.
conclusion: Quantum entanglement can enhance atom interferometry under realistic conditions, but finite temperature poses a significant challenge.

title: Symmetry-induced Logarithmic Relaxation In The Quantum Kicked Rotor
authors: Julien Hébraud, Floriane Arrouas, Bruno Peaudecerf, Juliette Billy, David Guéry-Odelin, Olivier Giraud, Bertrand Georgeot, Gabriel Lemarié And Christian Miniatura
abstract: We study the effect of discrete symmetries on coherent multiple scattering in the quantum kicked rotor. When the initial momentum is set to zero—as in recent Bose–Einstein condensate experiments—the effective pseudo-disorder becomes even under momentum inversion. The resulting discrete mirror symmetry of the dynamics profoundly alters spectral correlations: it generates quasi-degenerate Floquet doublets localised at opposite momenta, whose exponentially small splittings produce a hierarchy of exponentially large dynamical timescales. The coherent backscattering and forward-scattering peaks then exhibit a striking non-monotonic evolution and strongly asymmetric contrasts, followed by an exceptionally slow logarithmic relaxation toward a common asymptotic value—a hallmark of glassy dynamics, here emerging in a fully coherent quantum system. That such archetypal glass-like behaviour arises from a single discrete symmetry constraint reveals an unexpected and deep connection between quantum coherence and slow relaxation phenomena.
tldr: This paper shows that discrete mirror symmetry in the quantum kicked rotor leads to logarithmic relaxation, a glassy dynamics signature, in a fully coherent quantum system.
motivation: To understand how discrete symmetries affect coherent multiple scattering and spectral correlations in quantum systems, and to explore the emergence of glassy dynamics from simple symmetry constraints.
method: The authors study the quantum kicked rotor with zero initial momentum, where the effective pseudo-disorder becomes even under momentum inversion. They analyze spectral correlations, Floquet doublets, and the dynamics of coherent backscattering and forward-scattering peaks.
result: The mirror symmetry generates quasi-degenerate Floquet doublets with exponentially small splittings, leading to a hierarchy of timescales and a non-monotonic evolution of scattering peaks, culminating in an exceptionally slow logarithmic relaxation.
conclusion: A single discrete symmetry can produce archetypal glass-like relaxation in a coherent quantum system, revealing a deep connection between quantum coherence and slow dynamics.

motivation: Solid-state platforms for studying and controlling quantum chaos have been limited; bilayer graphene offers a tunable system.
method: The authors fabricate and measure stadium-shaped bilayer graphene cavities, tuning chaos via gate voltages and cavity shape.
result: They observe signatures of chaotic and regular dynamics, showing controllable transition between them.
conclusion: Bilayer graphene cavities provide a versatile platform for quantum chaos studies, with potential applications in quantum information.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: Presents PyOpticL, an open-source Python library for modular optical layout, demonstrated with a trapped-ion laser system achieving high-fidelity single-qubit gates.
motivation: Complex optical design in AMO experiments is not scalable due to piecewise setup; a modular, code-to-CAD approach is needed.
method: Developed PyOpticL with beam-path simulation and dynamic routing, enabling drop-in optical baseplates for common subsystems; demonstrated with a full laser system for strontium trapped ions.
result: Achieved over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates using 3D-printed baseplates, showing scalability and modularity.
conclusion: The open-source library and modular baseplates enable a new paradigm for designing and scaling optical systems in quantum computing and AMO physics.

title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: The paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into shape invariants and bosonic excitations, applied to lithium atom.
motivation: To characterize the information content of fermionic wave functions and identify robust few-particle entangled states.
method: Formal decomposition of wave function into fixed invariants (shapes) and variable bosonic excitations; applied to a benchmark lithium wave function.
result: The wave function is reduced to eleven shape blocks, five numerically significant, demonstrating superselection rules in configuration space.
conclusion: The decomposition provides a compact characterization and aids in finding robust entangled states in fermionic systems.

title: Experimental Exclusion Of A Generalized Károlyházy Gravity-induced Decoherence Model
authors: Nicola Bortolotti, Kristian Piscicchia, Alessio Porcelli, Matthias Laubenstein, Simone Manti, Antonino Marcianò, Federico Nola And Catalina Curceanu
abstract: We report new experimental constraints on the generalized version of the gravity-induced decoherence model originally proposed by Károlyházy. Using data collected by the VIP Collaboration at the INFN Gran Sasso National Laboratory with a high-purity germanium detector, we derive an improved lower bound on the spatial correlation length characterizing metric fluctuations in the model. We obtain a bound m (95% C.L.), which exceeds by more than an order of magnitude the previous experimental limit. When combined with the theoretical upper bound m derived from macroscopic localization requirements, our result excludes the generalized Károlyházy model. The same conclusion applies to an associated non-Markovian formulation of the continuous spontaneous localization model. Our findings significantly tighten experimental constraints on gravity-related decoherence scenarios and demonstrate the sensitivity of underground low-background experiments to foundational modifications of quantum mechanics.
tldr: Experimental exclusion of a gravity-induced decoherence model using underground detector data.
motivation: To test whether gravity causes wavefunction collapse, which is a foundational question in quantum mechanics.
method: Analysis of high-purity germanium detector data from the VIP Collaboration to constrain the spatial correlation length of metric fluctuations.
result: Improved lower bound on the correlation length by over an order of magnitude, excluding the generalized Károlyházy model.
conclusion: The model is ruled out, tightening constraints on gravity-related decoherence and spontaneous localization models.

title: A Maxwell Fish-eye Lens In A Bose–Einstein Condensate
authors: Jelte Duchêne, Elinor Kath, Floriane Arrouas, Hanyi Jang, Helmut Strobel, Markus K Oberthaler, Jay Mehta, Liam M Farrell, Wyatt Kirkby And Duncan H J O’dell
abstract: We experimentally realize an analogue of the optical Maxwell fish-eye lens (MFEL) using phononic excitations in a Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC). A MFEL is characterized by a radially symmetric, spatially varying refractive index with the remarkable property that rays emitted from any point within the lens are perfectly focused at their antipodal points. While the implementation of such gradient-index lenses is challenging in conventional optical systems, BECs offer a highly tunable platform in which the spatially varying speed of sound of collective excitations—phonons, the acoustic analogues of photons—can be engineered and their dynamics observed in real time. Time-resolved measurements of phonon wavefronts reveal focusing behavior that shows good agreement with analytical theory and numerical simulations. This work provides both a geometric and physical framework for engineering effective refractive indices using ultracold atoms, and simulating wave propagation on effective spherical geometries.
tldr: This paper experimentally realizes an analogue of the Maxwell fish-eye lens using phononic excitations in a Bose-Einstein condensate, demonstrating focusing of sound waves.
motivation: To create a highly tunable platform for studying gradient-index lenses and wave propagation on effective spherical geometries, which is challenging in conventional optics.
method: The authors engineer a spatially varying speed of sound in a BEC to mimic the refractive index profile of a Maxwell fish-eye lens, and observe phonon wavefront dynamics via time-resolved imaging.
result: Time-resolved measurements show focusing behavior that agrees well with analytical theory and numerical simulations.
conclusion: BECs provide a versatile analog system for simulating wave propagation in curved geometries and gradient-index optics.

title: Quantum Phases And Stability Of Bose–Hubbard Triangular Ladder With Magnetic Field
authors: Yue Jian, Jun-Hua Luo, Zi-Fa Yu, Juan Zhang, Ying-Ge Xu And Ju-Kui Xue
abstract: We investigate the ground state properties of interacting bosons on a triangular ladder subject to an artificial magnetic field. By means of the mean-field approximation, rich phases are revealed in the limit of weak interaction and large bosons occupation per site, including the Meissner superfluid, vortex superfluid, biased chiral superfluid (C-SF), C-SF and insulating phases. The quantum phases can be precisely identified and the underlying physics of phase transitions can be clarified by utilizing order parameters based on the atomic density, the effective rung current, and the current asymmetry ratio. Meanwhile, the phase transition of the system can be effectively controlled by adjusting the rung-to-leg coupling ratio, the magnetic flux and the atomic interaction. Furthermore, using Bogoliubov theory, we have mapped the stability phase diagram across all parameters, and clarified the interdependence between superfluidity and the dispersion relation. The excitation spectrum, which effectively describes the system’s energetic stability, is governed by the rung-to-leg coupling ratio, the magnetic flux, and the atomic interaction. Numerical simulations validate the dynamical instability of the system. This work offers a theoretical foundation for identifying new quantum phases exhibited by ultracold atoms in optical lattices and new experimental approaches for achieving system superfluidity.
tldr: This paper studies quantum phases and stability of a Bose-Hubbard triangular ladder in a magnetic field using mean-field and Bogoliubov theory.
motivation: To understand the ground state properties and phase transitions of interacting bosons on a triangular ladder under an artificial magnetic field.
method: Mean-field approximation and Bogoliubov theory are used to derive phase diagrams and excitation spectra.
result: Rich phases including Meissner superfluid, vortex superfluid, biased chiral superfluid, and insulating phases are identified; stability phase diagrams are mapped.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for identifying new quantum phases in ultracold atoms in optical lattices.

title: Anisotropic Fluorescence Signals Retarded Dipole-dipole Interactions In A Thermal Atomic Cloud
authors: Vyacheslav Shatokhin, Friedemann Landmesser, Mario Niebuhr, Frank Stienkemeier, Andreas Buchleitner And Lukas Bruder
abstract: We experimentally observe and theoretically explain anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals in the fluorescence from dilute thermal potassium vapours, at room temperature and particle densities . We identify the retarded part of the geometrically fully resolved inter-atomic, resonant dipole-dipole interaction as the crucial ingredient to theoretically reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
tldr: Experimental and theoretical study of anisotropic fluorescence signals from thermal atomic vapors due to retarded dipole-dipole interactions.
motivation: To understand the role of retarded dipole-dipole interactions in anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals observed in fluorescence from thermal atomic clouds.
method: Experimental observation of fluorescence from dilute thermal potassium vapors combined with theoretical modeling that includes the retarded part of the resonant dipole-dipole interaction.
result: The retarded dipole-dipole interaction is crucial to reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
conclusion: Retarded interactions must be considered to explain anisotropic fluorescence signals in thermal atomic ensembles.

title: Percolation With Coupled Lasers: Effect Of Non-linearities On The Phase Transition
authors: Simon Mahler, Nikita Stroev, Mahmoud Abu Rmilah, Asher Friesem And Nir Davidson
abstract: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are challenging due to difficulties in tuning site connectivity, isolating local interactions, and mitigating finite-size effects. In this work, we experimentally investigate percolation with a platform of coupled lasers, where connectivity, interaction strength, and system size can be controlled. Using a square array of lasers with astronomical number of possible cluster configurations, we show that the emergence of a percolating cluster corresponds to the onset of phase locking among the lasers. We also show that the percolation probability undergoes a second-order alike transition as a function of the site-occupation probability, with a threshold consistent with classical theoretical predictions. Surprisingly, we find that at low pump level, amplified mode competition (nonlinear regime) alters the effective behavior of the lasing sites and modify the nature of the percolation transition. The experimental results are interpreted by the means of a theoretical toy model with connectivity rules to the classical percolation.
tldr: This paper experimentally studies percolation using a coupled laser array, showing that the percolation transition corresponds to phase locking and that nonlinearities modify the transition.
motivation: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are challenging; the authors use a coupled laser platform to overcome these challenges and investigate the effect of nonlinearities.
method: A square array of coupled lasers with controllable connectivity and pump levels is used to observe percolation and phase locking, with a toy model to interpret results.
result: Percolation probability undergoes a second-order-like transition consistent with classical theory, but at low pump levels nonlinearities alter the effective behavior and modify the transition.
conclusion: The coupled laser platform enables controlled percolation studies, and nonlinearities can change the nature of the percolation transition.

title: Nonreciprocal Electrical Transport In Emerging Noncentrosymmetric Systems: From Hidden Symmetry To Functional Devices
authors: Shengyao Li, Zherui Yang, Xueyan Wang, Kian Ping Loh And X Renshaw Wang
abstract: Contrary to the reciprocal electrical transport constrained by the Onsager relations, nonreciprocal electrical transport arises in noncentrosymmetric systems where the resistance depends on the direction of current flow or external stimuli such as a magnetic field. Governed by symmetry-dependent charge dynamics, these responses appear as nonreciprocal charge transport (NCT) in the longitudinal direction and the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) in the transverse direction. Recent theoretical advances have expanded the range of mechanisms and material platforms capable of hosting nonreciprocal signals, revealing the role of hidden band-geometric properties. In parallel, experimental developments have exploited these effects for practical devices, offering promising alternatives to semiconductor-based rectifiers and wireless components, with advantages in broadband operation, ultrafast response, and high energy efficiency. In this review, we summarize electrical measurement techniques and characteristic transport signatures for identifying nonreciprocal phenomena and uncovering their underlying symmetry. We provide a comprehensive discussion of the fundamental mechanisms underlying NCT and NLHE, organized through representative material systems, and a subsequent examination of strategies for artificially inducing and enhancing nonreciprocity. Finally, we evaluate the technological perspectives of nonreciprocal electrical transport for electronic applications, along with key challenges and opportunities for scalable device implementation. By synthesizing current progress, this review aims to guide materials discovery and device innovation, and to inspire exploration of new symmetry settings and unconventional routes toward enhanced nonreciprocal functionalities.
tldr: A review of nonreciprocal electrical transport in noncentrosymmetric materials, focusing on symmetry-dependent charge dynamics and device applications.
motivation: To understand and harness nonreciprocal transport phenomena for next-generation electronic devices.
method: Summarizes experimental techniques and theoretical mechanisms for nonreciprocal charge transport and nonlinear Hall effect across various material systems.
result: Identifies hidden band-geometric properties and strategies to induce/enhance nonreciprocity.
conclusion: Nonreciprocal transport offers promising routes for broadband, ultrafast, energy-efficient devices, but challenges remain in scalable implementation.

title: Crystallography-driven Molecularization Of A Two-dimensional Spin- 3 / ...
authors: Hari Borutta, Tobias Müller, Ronny Thomale, Harald O Jeschke And Yasir Iqbal
abstract: Large-spin two-dimensional magnets are generally expected to develop conventional long-range order once the dominant exchange scale becomes appreciable. The layered spin- maple-leaf compound Na Mn O defies this expectation: despite sizable antiferromagnetic interactions and no evident disorder, it exhibits no magnetic ordering and displays two well-separated thermodynamic crossover scales. We show that this behavior originates from a crystallography-driven molecularization of the magnetic degrees of freedom. The low-symmetry structure partitions the Mn sublattice into inequivalent exchange pathways, generating a pronounced hierarchy that nearly isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons. Magnetic correlations therefore develop in two stages: first within individual hexagons at a scale set by the dominant exchange, and only at much lower temperatures do frustrated inter-hexagon couplings attempt to establish coherence across the lattice. While isolated hexagons reproduce the two-step thermodynamic structure, the experimentally relevant temperature scales emerge only once the hexagons are embedded in the frustrated two-dimensional network. The resulting quantum ground state is magnetically disordered, characterized by strong intra-hexagon correlations and rapidly decaying inter-hexagon correlations. These results identify crystallographic inequivalence as a materials-level mechanism for stabilizing molecularized and quantum-disordered states even in large-spin two-dimensional magnets.
tldr: This paper explains the absence of magnetic order in a large-spin 2D magnet via crystallography-driven molecularization into weakly coupled antiferromagnetic hexagons.
motivation: To understand why the layered spin-3/2 compound NaMn2O3 does not order magnetically despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions and no disorder.
method: The authors perform electronic structure calculations and model the magnetic system using a Heisenberg Hamiltonian with exchange couplings extracted from the crystal structure, then analyze the resulting spin model via classical and quantum methods.
result: The low-symmetry crystal structure creates a hierarchy of exchange couplings that nearly isolate antiferromagnetic hexagons, leading to two-stage magnetic correlations and a quantum-disordered ground state.
conclusion: Crystallographic inequivalence can stabilize molecularized and quantum-disordered states in large-spin 2D magnets, offering a new materials-level mechanism for frustration.

tldr: This paper reports a scanning tunneling microscope study of FeSe/SrTiO3, showing that tip-induced electric field can enhance superconductivity by involving the dz2 orbital and correlation effects.

title: Kovacs-like Memory Effect In Strain Stiffening Collagen Networks
authors: Maitri Mandal And Sayantan Majumdar Abhishek Ghadai
abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations. Such memory effects-reflecting parameters such as deformation direction, magnitude, and duration have been widely explored in soft amorphous solids. Here, we report a Kovacs-like memory effect manifested as a non-monotonic stress relaxation in vitro biopolymer networks formed by type-I collagen, an essential component of the mammalian extracellular matrix. Using shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging, we find that this memory effect emerges exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, and persists over a much broader range of strain amplitudes than previously reported for other viscoelastic amorphous materials. Furthermore, we uncover a strong correlation between the memory response and the development of negative normal stresses and associated strain fields, highlighting the unique nonequilibrium mechanics underlying memory formation in biopolymer networks.
tldr: This paper reports a Kovacs-like memory effect in strain-stiffening collagen networks, focusing on non-equilibrium mechanics of biopolymer networks.
motivation: To understand memory effects in soft amorphous materials, specifically in biopolymer networks like collagen, which are important for biological tissues.
method: Shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging to observe stress relaxation and normal stress development in collagen networks under nonlinear strain-stiffening conditions.
result: A non-monotonic stress relaxation (Kovacs-like memory effect) is observed exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, correlated with negative normal stresses and strain fields.
conclusion: The memory effect in collagen networks arises from unique nonequilibrium mechanics distinct from other amorphous materials, with potential implications for biological tissue mechanics.

title: Direct Visualization Of Field-driven Valence Band Modulation In Electrostatically Reconfigured Graphene Devices
authors: Umidakhon Rayimjonova, Chin-Yi Huang, Yi-Cheng Weng, Elin Cartwright, Fredrik O L Johansson, Noemi Vannucchi, Pavel Dudin, Avila Jose, Pei Ding, David Muradas-Belinchón, Henry Nameirakpam, Zhaojun Li, Andreas Lindblad And M Venkata Kamalakar
abstract: Graphene with ultrathin metal-oxide layers has emerged as a scalable platform for integrated electronic, spintronic, and neuromorphic devices. The in-plane electric fields in such devices are typically inferred indirectly from transport measurements, which do not provide microscopic details of the interface potential profile. Here, we use photoemission microscopy to uncover the precise electrostatic landscape of a complete device comprising diverse, heterogeneous ultrathin metal-oxide-covered graphene junctions. Using in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution, we directly image the real potential profile across an entire graphene device, including regions covered by AlOx and TiOx nanometer-thick overlayers. Tracking the valence band edge under current bias and gate voltage enables quantitative analysis of internal field evolution via a spectroscopic screening factor, revealing an up to more than 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene covered with oxides, in agreement with transport measurements. title: Orthogonal Phase Modulation And Lissajous Mode Decoupling In Light-induced Thermoelastic Spectroscopy For Real-time Multi-component Gas Sensing

abstract: This paper proposed an optical detection mechanism that utilized orthogonal phase modulation (OPM) and Lissajous mode decoupling within a light-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy (LITES) sensor for the first time, enabling real-time multi-component gas sensing. By establishing a two-dimensional forced vibration model of a quartz tuning fork (QTF) under dual-path OPM, it revealed the vibration mode coupling mechanism induced by non-ideal phase and amplitude conditions, thereby providing a theoretical basis and optimization pathway for suppressing channel crosstalk. In the OPM-LITES sensor, two continuous-wave distributed feedback lasers were modulated by sinusoidal waves with the same frequency (f0/2, where f0 is the resonant frequency of the QTF) but a phase difference of 45°. The combined beam, after wavelength division multiplexing, co-excited the self-designed low-frequency QTF. The piezoelectric signal generated by the QTF underwent orthogonal demodulation via a lock-in amplifier (LIA). The concentration information for the two gases was independently retrieved from the decoupled X-component and Y-component of the LIA. Experimental results demonstrated that the OPM-LITES sensor exhibited excellent linear responses to both methane (CH4) and acetylene (C2H2), with average relative systematic errors of 0.54% and 0.79%, and maximum relative errors of 1.72% and 1.38%, respectively. Allan deviation analysis indicated that the minimum detection limits (MDLs) for CH4 and C2H2 reached 0.32 ppm and 0.29 ppm, with normalized noise-equivalent absorption coefficients of 5.09 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2 and 6.18 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2, respectively. This study not only provided a simple and efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection but also established a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling and signal processing in spectroscopic sensing.

conclusion: The proposed OPM-LITES sensor provides a simple, efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection with a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling.
